projects.name: apicheck
projects.tagline: A read-only web and API misconfiguration checker: headers, cookies, CORS, leftover sensitive files, directory listing, verbose errors, and endpoints that answer without authentication.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: Most of the mistakes that turn into real incidents aren't exotic — they're a missing header, an exposed .env, or an endpoint nobody remembered to lock down. This checks for the common ones quickly, so the interesting manual work can start sooner.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Web and API testing: the exact class of low-hanging misconfiguration that shows up in almost every real assessment, automated into one pass.
  • A checker that knows the difference between "indicator" and "proof": every finding says where to look, not that a vulnerability is confirmed, and soft-404 sites are detected and excluded from the exposure check to avoid false positives.
  • Tested against both a deliberately misconfigured server and a hardened one, so it's shown to flag the first and stay quiet on the second — not just to run without crashing.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer
  • No third-party packages — standard library only
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/apicheck
cd apicheck
python3 -m apicheck --help

No pip install needed.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Basic scan of a lab target

python3 -m apicheck http://192.168.1.10:8080

Compare an authenticated vs. anonymous response on specific endpoints

python3 -m apicheck http://192.168.1.10:8080 --token eyJhbGciOi... --endpoints paths.txt

Write a report

python3 -m apicheck http://192.168.1.10:8080 -o report.md
python3 -m apicheck http://192.168.1.10:8080 -o report.json

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
FlagWhat it doesDefault
urlBase URL, e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080required
--tokenBearer token; compares authenticated vs. anonymous responsesoff
--endpointsFile of one path per line, tested for missing authenticationoff
--timeoutRequest timeout, secondstool default
--authorizedConfirm written permission for a public targetrequired for public IPs
-o, --outWrite the report to .md or .jsonstdout

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
$ python3 -m apicheck http://192.168.1.10:4280
apicheck: only test systems you own or have written permission to test.
# apicheck report: http://192.168.1.10:4280

Requests sent: 28. Findings: 9.

## [MEDIUM] Content-Security-Policy missing
...
## [MEDIUM] Cookie 'PHPSESSID' lacks HttpOnly, SameSite
...

sections.label: What it checks
sections.html:
CheckLooks for
headersMissing CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy; version strings in Server/X-Powered-By
cookiesSession cookies missing HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite
corsAccess-Control-Allow-Origin reflecting an arbitrary origin, especially combined with credentials
methodsTRACE enabled; risky methods (PUT, DELETE, PATCH) advertised via OPTIONS
exposureLeftover .git/HEAD, .env, backup files, phpinfo.php, server-status, published API docs
listingDirectory listing enabled on common paths
errorsStack traces or SQL error text leaking from a malformed request
authEndpoints (from --endpoints or auto-discovered via an OpenAPI/Swagger document) that return the same data with and without a bearer token

Pages that answer 200 to everything (soft-404 sites) are detected and excluded from the exposure check, to avoid false positives.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

13 tests spin up two local servers — one deliberately misconfigured, one hardened — and assert the checker flags the first and stays quiet on the second. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• This is a checker, not an exploit tool: every finding is an indicator to verify by hand, not proof that a vulnerability exists.
  • Read-only, GET-based checks; it doesn't attempt authentication bypass or injection itself.
  • The auth check compares response shape with and without a token; it can miss subtler authorization bugs (e.g. one user reading another user's data at the same auth level).

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. A public target needs --authorized.

sections.label: License
sections.html: MIT. See LICENSE.

projects.name: reconkit
projects.tagline: Threaded port scan, HTTP/security-header probing and optional subdomain brute force, in one Markdown or JSON report. Standard library only.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: Recon is the first phase of almost every test: map what's listening, what's running, and what's misconfigured, before anything else. This started as a handful of one-off scripts I kept rewriting for labs, so I turned it into one small tool with tests.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Recon and enumeration: the port scan, HTTP probe and subdomain brute force an engagement starts with, as one tool instead of three separate scripts.
  • Writing tooling that holds up under test, not just under a demo: 8 unit tests, all run against a local server so nothing touches the network, with CI on three Python versions.
  • A scope guard built into the tool itself, not left to the operator to remember: a public target is refused without --authorized.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer
  • No third-party packages — standard library only
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/reconkit
cd reconkit
python3 -m reconkit --help

No pip install needed.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Top common ports and an HTTP probe, against a lab host

python3 -m reconkit 192.168.1.10

Specific ports, written as a Markdown report

python3 -m reconkit 192.168.1.10 -p 22,80,443,8000-8100 -o report.md

JSON output, for feeding into another tool

python3 -m reconkit 192.168.1.10 -o report.json

Subdomain brute force

python3 -m reconkit example.com -w wordlists/small.txt --authorized

One word per line in the wordlist. --authorized is required for any public (non-private) address — reconkit refuses to scan one otherwise.

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
FlagWhat it doesDefault
targetHostname or IP to scanrequired
-p, --portstop, or a list like 22,80,8000-8100top
-w, --wordlistSubdomain wordlist; enables brute forceoff
--timeoutPer-port connect timeout, secondstool default
--no-httpSkip the HTTP probeoff
--authorizedConfirm written permission to test a public targetrequired for public IPs
-o, --outWrite the report to this file (.md or .json by extension)stdout

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
$ python3 -m reconkit 192.168.1.10 -p 22,80,4280
reconkit: only scan systems you own or have written permission to test.
# Recon report: 192.168.1.10

Resolved address: `192.168.1.10`

## Open ports

| Port | Service | Banner |
|---|---|---|
| 22  | ssh  | SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 |
| 4280 | unknown | - |

## Web services

- http://192.168.1.10:4280: HTTP 200, title "Login :: DVWA", server `Apache/2.4.69`, missing headers: ...

sections.label: What it checks
sections.html:
CheckWhat it does
Port scanThreaded TCP connect scan over a top-ports list or a custom range, with a short banner grab for non-HTTP ports
HTTP probeFor every web port found (and silent unknown ports), fetches the page title, Server header, and checks for the six standard security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, etc.)
Subdomain brute forceResolves word.domain for a wordlist, with wildcard-DNS detection so a catch-all record doesn't produce hundreds of false hits
Scope checkRefuses a public IP unless --authorized is passed

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

8 tests, all against a local test server — nothing reaches the network. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• Port scan is TCP connect only, not SYN; it's slower than a raw-socket scanner but needs no elevated privileges.
  • Banner grabbing is best-effort and may miss services that don't respond to a bare connection.
  • Wildcard-DNS detection catches a catch-all A record; it won't catch every form of subdomain takeover or wildcard TLS cert.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. The scope check enforces this for public targets; it does not replace having actual authorization.

sections.label: License
sections.html: MIT. See LICENSE.

projects.name: Arjun
projects.tagline: An HTTP parameter discovery tool: sends a huge wordlist against an endpoint and reports which parameter names actually change the response.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: Plenty of endpoints accept a parameter nobody documented: a debug flag, an old filter, an admin switch left in from testing. Arjun finds those by sending a large wordlist of likely names and watching for any response that looks different from the baseline. This fork keeps that approach and fixes the parts where "look different" or "load the targets" quietly did the wrong thing.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Web and API testing: parameter discovery is a normal step before fuzzing or exploiting an endpoint, and this is a tool I run for it, not just read the code of.
  • Finding bugs by reproducing them first, not guessing from a bug title: every fix below starts with a script that triggers the exact failure before any line of the fix is written. See What changed.
  • Tracing a crash back through the actual call chain (--import burp.xml → importer() → requester()) instead of patching the symptom at the point it happened to surface.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer (CI runs 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; also run by hand on 3.13 and 3.14)
  • requests, dicttoxml, ratelimit (see requirements.txt)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
Arch Linux

sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/Arjun.git
cd Arjun
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/Arjun.git
cd Arjun
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

Check it worked:

arjun -h

The virtual environment only needs activating in the shell you use it from. Run deactivate, or open a new terminal, to leave it.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Scan one URL

arjun -u https://example.com/api/userinfo

Sends the default wordlist (25,890 names) against the URL and prints any parameter that changes the response.

Scan a list of URLs

arjun -i urls.txt -oT found.txt

One URL per line. -oT writes url?param=value for every parameter found, one per line.

Replay captured requests from Burp

arjun -i export.xml -oJ found.json

Imports every request Burp exported as XML, including its captured body, and tests each one.

Send data in every request

arjun -u https://example.com/api/search -m JSON --include '{"q": "test"}'

Keeps q present on every probe, for an endpoint that 400s without it.

Through Burp or another proxy

arjun -u https://example.com --headers "Cookie: SESSION=abc123"

Use a smaller, faster wordlist

arjun -u https://example.com -w my_params.txt -t 10

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
FlagWhat it doesDefault
-u URLTarget URLnone
-i [FILE]Import targets: URL list, raw request, or Burp XML exportnone
-o, -oJ FILEWrite findings as JSONoff
-oT FILEWrite findings as plain text (url?param=value)off
-oB [HOST:PORT]Send findings to Burp's proxyoff
-w FILEWordlist of parameter namesbundled 25,890-name list
-m METHODGET, POST, JSON or XMLGET
-t NConcurrent threads5
-d SECONDSDelay between requests0
-T SECONDSPer-request timeout15
-c NParameters sent per request (chunk size)auto
-qQuiet modeoff
--rate-limit NMax requests per second9999
--headers [HEADERS]Extra request headersbrowser-style defaults
--include DATAJSON object or query string sent with every requestnone
--stablePrefer reliability over speed on a flaky targetoff
--disable-redirectsDon't follow redirectsoff
--casing STYLEParameter casing: like_this, likeThis, likethislike_this
--passive [SOURCE]Pull extra names from Wayback, CommonCrawl, OTXoff

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
Against a local test server with a hidden secret_admin_flag parameter:

[*] Scanning 0/1: http://127.0.0.1:33225/
[*] Probing the target for stability
[*] Analysing HTTP response for anomalies
[*] Logicforcing the URL endpoint
[✓] parameter detected: secret_admin_flag, based on: body length
[+] Parameters found: secret_admin_flag

-oJ for the same run:

{
    "http://127.0.0.1:33225/": {
        "headers": { "...": "..." },
        "method": "GET",
        "params": ["secret_admin_flag"]
    }
}

sections.label: How it works
sections.html: Arjun first probes the target to get a baseline response, then sends the wordlist in chunks (binary-search style, narrowing on the chunk that changed something) rather than one parameter per request, so it can go through tens of thousands of names in a small number of requests. A chunk is flagged if the response's status code, headers, body length, or reflected text differ from the baseline; flagged chunks are split and retested until a single parameter is isolated.

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream s0md3v/ArjunThis fork
--import on a file with a leading blank line or commentReturns no targets, silentlySkips blank lines and finds the real format
-i urls.txt --include '...'--include is silently ignored (wrong dict key)Applied to every request
-i export.xml (Burp) on a request with a bodyCrashes: ValueError: dictionary update sequence element #0 has length 1; 2 is requiredBody is parsed into parameters and sent normally
--include 'a=1&flag&b=2'The stray flag token wipes a and b too; --include becomes {}Only the bad token is skipped
Requests that rely on requester()'s default payloadA mutable default dict is shared and mutated across every call that omits itEach call starts from a clean dict
A target that replies with text/plain or no Content-TypeRejected as "not a webpage"Accepted; only binary/media Content-Types are rejected
Automated testsNone14 tests, run in CI

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: --import silently returning nothing on a leading blank line

importer() picked an import format by reading lines one at a time and returning [] unconditionally as soon as a line didn't start with <?xml, http(s)://, GET or POST — including a blank line, which real target-list files often start with. Reproduced with a two-URL file that had one leading blank line: importer() returned [] for it and a plain list of the same two URLs with no leading blank line correctly returned two requests. Blank lines are now skipped before the format is checked; a genuinely unrecognised first line still returns [].

Fixed: --include ignored for -i urls.txt imports

urls_import() built each request dict with the key 'data', but requester() only ever reads request['include']. Every --include value passed alongside -i urls.txt was silently dropped; only single-URL (-u) scans actually used it. The key is now 'include', parsed through the same parse_params() used everywhere else.

Fixed: -i export.xml crashing on any captured request with a body

burp_import() took the raw captured HTTP request body (a string like username=admin&password=secret) and stored it directly as request['include']. requester() then calls payload.update(request['include']) on it, and dict.update() on a string iterates its characters — each a length-1 string — and raises ValueError: dictionary update sequence element #0 has length 1; 2 is required. Reproduced by importing a one-item Burp XML export with a POST body: the import crashed before a single request was sent. The body is now parsed into a parameter dict before being stored.

Fixed: a bad --include token silently discarding everything parsed before it

The query-string branch of get_params() built up params one &-separated token at a time, and on any token without an = (a bare flag, or a stray trailing &) it caught the resulting IndexError by resetting params = {} — discarding every parameter already parsed, not just the bad token. Reproduced with a=1&b=2&flag&c=3: upstream returns {'c': '3'}, losing a and b. This parsing logic moved into a new arjun/core/parsing.py (shared by utils.py and importer.py, which needed it too) and now skips only the one malformed token.

Fixed: requester()'s mutable default argument

def requester(request, payload={}) evaluates {} once, at import time, and every call that omits payload reuses and mutates that same dict via payload.update(...). No current call site omits it, but it's a real foot-gun for anyone using requester() as a library function (which the new test suite does) or for a future call site that relies on the default. payload is now None by default, with a fresh dict created per call. payload.update() is also now guarded to only run when include is actually a dict, so a caller that still hands it a raw string gets ignored instead of crashing.

Fixed: legitimate non-HTML/JSON/XML targets rejected as "not a webpage"

stable_request() only accepted a response whose Content-Type contained text, html, json or xml, rejecting everything else outright — including text/plain, a missing Content-Type header, or application/x-www-form-urlencoded, all of which real APIs return. This is now a blocklist of actually-binary types (image/, video/, audio/, font/, application/pdf, application/zip, application/octet-stream and a few others) instead of an allowlist, so an unusual-but-text target is scanned instead of skipped.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
pip install -r requirements.txt pytest
pytest -q

14 tests. A local HTTP server backs the requester()/stable_request() tests; the importer and parsing tests use real file fixtures (including a Burp-XML-shaped one) with no network access. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• Still a wordlist-based tool: a parameter not in -w's list (or --passive's sources) won't be found.
  • Anomaly detection compares status code, headers, body length and reflected text; a parameter that changes something else (a side effect with no visible response difference) won't be caught.
  • --rate-limit's ceiling is read once, at import time, from the CLI argument — it can't be changed after the process starts.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only scan targets you own or have written permission to test. Arjun sends a large number of requests per target; --rate-limit, --stable and -d exist to keep that polite.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on s0md3v/Arjun by Somdev Sangwan and contributors. Upstream's wordlist, anomaly-detection approach and chunking strategy are theirs. The fixes and tests above are in this fork.

sections.label: License
sections.html: AGPL-3.0, the same as upstream. See LICENSE.

projects.name: Corsy
projects.tagline: A CORS misconfiguration scanner: sends crafted Origin headers and reports the ones the server trusts.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: Cross-origin resource sharing is easy to get wrong: a server that echoes back whatever Origin it is sent, or trusts null, lets any website read responses meant for logged-in users. Corsy tries the known ways a CORS allow-list gets bypassed and tells you which one the target falls for. This fork keeps that, and fixes the parts that gave wrong or missing answers in real use.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Web and API testing: CORS misconfiguration is a standard part of an API assessment, and this is a tool I actually run for it.
  • Finding a real concurrency bug by testing under load, not just reading the code: the fix for threaded scans corrupting each other's findings was reproduced before it was fixed. See What changed.
  • Noticing when a tool's own output can't be trusted (a failed request looked identical to a clean host) and fixing the gap instead of only adding features.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer (CI runs 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; also run by hand on 3.14)
  • requests 2.25+ and urllib3 1.26+ (see requirements.txt)
  • nano, only if you use --headers with no value (it opens an editor; Unix only)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
Arch Linux

sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/Corsy.git
cd Corsy
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/Corsy.git
cd Corsy
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Check it worked:

python3 corsy.py --version

The virtual environment only needs activating in the shell you use it from. Run deactivate, or open a new terminal, to leave it.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Scan one URL

python3 corsy.py -u https://example.com/api/me

Sends the probes to that URL and prints any misconfiguration found.

Scan a list of URLs

python3 corsy.py -i urls.txt -o results.json

One URL or bare hostname per line (example.com is treated as https://example.com). Blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped. -o saves the findings as JSON.

Pipe targets in from another tool

cat urls.txt | python3 corsy.py
subfinder -d example.com | httprobe | python3 corsy.py -t 10

Piped targets are merged with -u and -i, and duplicates are removed.

Send traffic through Burp

python3 corsy.py -u https://example.com --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080

Authenticated scans

python3 corsy.py -u https://example.com/api/me --headers "Cookie: SESSION=abc123\nUser-Agent: Mozilla/5.0"

Headers are separated by a literal \n.

Gate a CI job

python3 corsy.py -i staging-urls.txt --fail-on-finding -q

Exits 1 if anything is found, 0 if clean, so a pipeline can fail on it.

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
FlagWhat it doesDefault
-u URLTarget URLnone
-i FILEFile of URLs or hostnamesnone
-o FILEWrite findings as JSONoff
-t NNumber of threads2
-d SECONDSDelay between requests0
--timeout SECONDSPer-request timeout10
--proxy URLRoute requests through a proxyoff
--headers [HEADERS]Extra request headers; no value opens an editorbuilt-in browser headers
-qHide description, severity and exploitation textoff
--fail-on-findingExit 1 when a misconfiguration is foundoff
-V, --versionPrint the version

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
Against a local test server that reflects every Origin:

 + http://127.0.0.1:8911/reflect
   - Class: origin reflected
   - Description: This host allows any origin to make requests to it.
   - Severity: high
   - Exploitation: Make requests from any domain you control.
   - ACAO Header: http://example.com
   - ACAC Header: true

ACAO is Access-Control-Allow-Origin and ACAC is Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. A reflected origin with ACAC: true means another site can read authenticated responses.

sections.label: What it checks
sections.html:
CheckSeverityWhat it means
origin reflectedhighAny Origin is echoed back
pre-domain wildcardhighA host that ends with the target's name is accepted
post-domain wildcardhighA host that starts with the target's name is accepted
null origin allowedhighThe null Origin is trusted
unescaped regexhighThe allow-list regex has an unescaped dot
unrecognized underscorehighAn underscore in the Origin bypasses validation
broken parserhighA backtick in the Origin bypasses validation
third party allowedmediumA different host is trusted
wildcard valuelow* is returned (browsers won't send credentials with it)
http origin allowedlowAn unencrypted http:// Origin is trusted

sections.label: How it works
sections.html: For each URL, Corsy sends GET requests with a different Origin header each time: the site's own origin first, then a third-party origin, then variations of the site's name (prefixed, suffixed, with an underscore, a backtick, an altered dot) and null. If the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoes back an origin it shouldn't trust, that's a finding. If the first probe shows the server sends no CORS headers at all, it stops there.

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream s0md3v/CorsyThis fork
Two findings of the same kind scanned togetherShare one record, so their ACAO/ACAC values overwrite each otherEach finding has its own copy
-i and -u when stdin isn't a terminal (CI, cron, a subprocess)Ignored; only stdin is readMerged with piped targets
Request timeoutNone; one dead host can hang a thread forever--timeout, default 10 s
A request that failsOnly a refused connection printed anything; every other failure was silent, so the host looked cleanEvery failure is reported
Where it finds its checks databaseBuilt from sys.path[0], which breaks when Corsy is imported rather than run as a scriptRelative to the package
Proxy (Burp)None--proxy
Use in CIAlways exits 0--fail-on-finding exits 1 on a finding
Hostnames without a schemeSkippedTreated as https://
Automated testsNone9 tests, run in CI

Use something else when you need preflight (OPTIONS) coverage or session-aware testing: Corsy only sends GET requests.

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: findings overwrote each other when scanned in parallel

Every result of the same kind was built from one shared record loaded from db/details.json, and the scanner wrote the headers into that record. With more than one thread, two endpoints of the same class ended up reporting identical ACAO and ACAC values. Reproduced with two wildcard endpoints, one sending Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and one not: every run reported them as the same. A credentialed wildcard could be reported as not credentialed, or the reverse. Each finding now gets its own copy. A regression test runs both endpoints concurrently five times.

Fixed: -i and -u were ignored when stdin wasn't a terminal

When stdin was not a TTY, Corsy read targets from stdin only. In CI, cron or any subprocess, -i urls.txt printed "No valid URLs to test" even with a valid file. It now merges -u, -i and piped targets, and removes duplicates.

Fixed: failed requests looked like clean hosts

The request wrapper printed a message only for a refused connection and returned nothing for any other failure, including a redirect loop (it compared against a string that never appears in the error). A host that failed to answer was therefore indistinguishable from a host with no misconfiguration. Failures are now caught by type and reported. There was also no timeout, so a host that accepted a connection and never answered blocked its thread indefinitely. --timeout adds one.

Fixed: the checks database path

It was built from sys.path[0], which is empty when Corsy is imported rather than run as a script, so importing it failed with FileNotFoundError: /db/details.json. The path is now resolved from the package's own location.

Added: --proxy, --fail-on-finding, --version, bare hostnames

Proxying through Burp, a non-zero exit for CI, a version flag, and acceptance of example.com style input with # comments and blank lines skipped.

Housekeeping

core/requester.py mixed tabs and spaces in one block. It parsed fine, so this isn't a bug fix; it was just tidied while the file was being rewritten.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
pip install pytest
pytest -q

Nine tests start a small local HTTP server that models each misconfiguration and assert that the scanner finds it, that a clean host returns nothing, that two findings never share state, that a hung host times out, and that input parsing behaves. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13. Nothing leaves your machine.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• GET requests only. It does not send preflight OPTIONS requests.
  • It reports the first misconfiguration it finds on a URL and stops, so a URL with two problems shows one.
  • invalid value appears in the checks database and in upstream's list of tests, but no code ever emits it, so Corsy effectively runs 10 checks, not 11.
  • It sends no cookies or tokens unless you pass --headers, so it tests the anonymous view of an endpoint unless you give it a session.
  • TLS certificates are not verified, so scans work against lab hosts with self-signed certs.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. Each scan sends up to nine requests per URL.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on s0md3v/Corsy by Somdev Sangwan and contributors. Upstream's detection logic and checks database are theirs. The fixes and additions above are in this fork.

sections.label: License
sections.html: GPL-3.0, the same as upstream. See LICENSE.

projects.name: jwt_tool
projects.tagline: Decodes, tampers with, signs and attacks JSON Web Tokens: the toolkit for testing whether a JWT implementation actually checks what it claims to.
projects.license: GPL-3.0 (upstream's own licence file; see License)

sections.label: Why
sections.html: JWTs carry authentication and authorization state, and a surprising number of implementations accept a token they shouldn't: no signature, the wrong algorithm, a key swapped for a public one. jwt_tool automates the standard checks for that class of bug, scans a live endpoint's behaviour with different tampered tokens, and helps forge a new one once a weakness is found.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Web and API testing: this is the tool I reach for whenever an engagement touches authentication tokens, and this fork is what I use.
  • Reading and fixing someone else's code under real constraints: four independent crashes diagnosed from a 2,200-line single file, each reproduced with a crafted token before being fixed, not patched blind. See What changed.
  • Writing tests that prove a fix instead of just exercising the code: the suite below drives the real CLI against each crash case and asserts it no longer happens.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.11 or newer (CI runs 3.11, 3.12, 3.13; 3.14 verified by hand, see below)
  • pycryptodomex, requests, termcolor, ratelimit (see requirements.txt)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
Arch Linux

sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/jwt_tool.git
cd jwt_tool
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/jwt_tool.git
cd jwt_tool
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Check it worked. The first run also creates ~/.jwt_tool/jwtconf.ini and a set of test keys:

python3 jwt_tool.py -h

Docker

Upstream also publishes a Docker image; this fork's fixes aren't built into it (yet), so for now use the source install above if you want this fork's behaviour.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Read a token's claims

python3 jwt_tool.py eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0IiwibmFtZSI6ImFsaWNlIiwicm9sZSI6InVzZXIiLCJpYXQiOjE3MDAwMDAwMDB9.R11xpZc8uimaZMTBmvRCRII-HPbxcVI8QDSKR-DF7EU

Decodes the header and payload and flags any timestamp claim.

Run a playbook scan against a live endpoint

python3 jwt_tool.py -t https://example.com/api/me -rc "session=<token>" -M pb

Replays the request with a battery of tampered tokens (alg:none, blank signature, key confusion, and more) and reports which ones the server still accepts.

Tamper a claim and re-sign

python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -I -pc role -pv admin -S hs256 -p secret

Injects role: admin into the payload and signs the result with a known HMAC secret.

Crack a weak HMAC secret

python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -C -d jwt-common.txt

Tries every line of the bundled wordlist as the signing secret.

Route a live check through Burp

python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -t https://example.com/api/me -M pb -P 127.0.0.1:8080

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
The tool has a large flag set (tampering, signing, exploits, cracking); the most-used ones:

FlagWhat it doesDefault
jwtThe token to work with (or read it from -r/cookies/headers)none
-t, --targeturl URLSend the forged token to this URLnone
-rc, --cookiesCookies to send with the requestnone
-M, --modeScan mode: pb playbook, er fuzz claims for errors, cc fuzz common claims, at all testsnone
-X, --exploitA known attack: a alg:none, n null signature, b blank password, k key confusion, i inject JWKS, s spoof JWKSnone
-I, --injectclaimsAdd or change claims (combine with -pc/-pv/-hc/-hv)off
-S, --signSign the result: hs256/rs256/es256/ps256 and 384/512 variantsnone
-C, --crackBrute-force an HMAC secret (combine with -d/-p/-kf)off
-np, --noproxyDisable the proxy for this runoff
-P, --proxy HOST:PORT*(this fork)* Set the proxy for this runconfig's proxy value
-v, --verboseSlightly more detail while parsingoff

Run python3 jwt_tool.py -h for the complete list; the exploit and sign options in particular have several sub-modes worth reading in full before using them live.

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
Dissecting a sample HS256 token (sub, name, role, iat):

Token header values:
[+] alg = "HS256"
[+] typ = "JWT"

Token payload values:
[+] sub = "1234"
[+] name = "alice"
[+] role = "user"
[+] iat = 1700000000    ==> TIMESTAMP = 2023-11-15 03:13:20 (UTC)

sections.label: How it works
sections.html: jwt_tool decodes the token locally (no network needed for that), then either tampers with the decoded claims and re-encodes/re-signs it, or sends a battery of tampered variants to a live URL and compares responses to tell which tampering the server accepted. The scan modes in -M run a fixed set of known JWT weaknesses; -X runs one specific exploit by name; -I/-T give manual control over which claim changes and how the result is signed.

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream ticarpi/jwt_toolThis fork
Python 3.14Crashes on first run: can't write its own config fileFixed
A token with a nested object or array claim (e.g. Firebase's firebase.identities)Crashes with TypeErrorFixed
iat/exp as a date string, or a huge out-of-range valueCrashes with ValueError/OverflowErrorShown as-is, no crash
Setting the proxy for one runEdit jwtconf.ini first-P/--proxy
Automated testsNone7 tests, run in CI

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: the tool couldn't create its config file on Python 3.14 (upstream #142)

Config generation stored its inline help text as INI keys, several of which contain a : ("# To disable the proxy option set this value to: False..."). Python 3.14 tightened configparser to reject writing a key that contains its own delimiter character, so the very first run crashed with InvalidWriteError before a usable config existed. Reproduced by running the tool fresh under Python 3.14. Fixed by writing that guidance as a real comment block above the config instead of smuggling it into key names; nothing in the text was lost.

Fixed: crashes on nested or list-shaped claims (upstream #115, #135)

A payload with a nested object — Firebase tokens are the common real example, with firebase.identities.email as a list inside a dict inside a claim — crashed with TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not OrderedDict. The renderer that walks a claim's sub-values called a string-casting helper on values that were already parsed Python objects, and that helper always tried json.loads() on its input regardless of type. Reproduced with a crafted token carrying a nested dict-of-list claim. Fixed in two places: the helper now returns non-string input unchanged, and the nested-claim renderer prints any depth of object or array with json.dumps(..., indent=4) instead of a one-level-only loop.

Fixed: crashes on timestamp claims that aren't a plain number (upstream #95, #113)

iat, nbf and exp were assumed to always be a clean Unix integer. A date string (seen in the wild, e.g. "07/05/2023 14:17:40") raised ValueError; a value far outside the range Python's datetime can represent raised OverflowError or OSError, depending on platform. Either crash ends the whole run on an otherwise-decodable token. Reproduced with both shapes of bad input. Fixed with a try/except around the parse: a claim that can't be read as a timestamp is now printed as its raw value instead of stopping the tool, and a claim that parses fine still gets the timestamp and expiry check exactly as before.

Added: -P/--proxy to set the proxy for one run (upstream #104)

The proxy was config-file only; changing it for a single run meant editing jwtconf.ini by hand. -P host:port overrides it for just that invocation, the same way -np already disabled it for one run. Verified against a local HTTP listener standing in for Burp: requests sent with -P arrived at the listener in absolute-URI form; the same command without it did not.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
pip install pytest
pytest -q

Seven tests run the real jwt_tool.py as a subprocess (an isolated $HOME so the real config is never touched) against crafted tokens: nested/Firebase-style claims, a string-date timestamp, an out-of-range timestamp, a list claim, a normal token with valid expiry, and the -P flag. Each asserts the process produces no traceback. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13. Python 3.14 support (the #142 fix) was additionally verified by hand, since no CI runner currently ships it.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• The test suite checks that the four fixed crashes no longer happen and that ordinary tokens still decode correctly. It doesn't cover the rest of this file's 2,200 lines (the sign, exploit and crack paths), which are upstream's long-standing, separately-tested logic.
  • -C/crack speed depends entirely on the wordlist; it does not brute-force arbitrary secrets.
  • Live scanning (-t/-M) sends real HTTP requests to whatever URL you give it.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only point -t/-M/live scanning at systems you own or have written permission to test. Cracking, tampering and exploit modes are for testing tokens you're authorized to attack.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on ticarpi/jwt_tool by Ted Rowland (ticarpi) and contributors. The scan modes, exploit catalogue, signing and cracking logic are upstream's work; the fixes and the proxy flag above are this fork's.

sections.label: License
sections.html: GPL-3.0, the same as upstream. See LICENSE.

projects.name: King Phisher
projects.tagline: A phishing-campaign toolkit for security-awareness testing, kept running on a current Python after upstream stopped maintaining it.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: King Phisher runs phishing-simulation campaigns to measure and improve an organisation's real-world susceptibility, with a GUI client, a server, and template-driven emails and landing pages. Upstream has said outright it's no longer maintained, and the maintainer confirmed on an open issue that King Phisher 2.0 is a from-scratch rewrite carrying none of this codebase over — so nothing broken here was going to get fixed. This fork fixes what's actually broken on a current Python, without touching the campaign logic or the GTK client UI.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Social engineering: this is the toolkit I use for authorized phishing-simulation campaigns, and this fork is why it still runs.
  • Diagnosing a dead import chain down to the exact removed stdlib module, then rebuilding the affected code on its modern replacement instead of patching around it.
  • Verifying a fix actually works end-to-end (a real SMTP client, not just "it imports now") — see What changed.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.12 or newer for the server/dev side this fork touches
  • System packages for the full client+server install: GTK, PostgreSQL (handled by tools/install.sh)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
Two paths: the full install (GTK client + server, needs system packages), or just the Python/dev side this fork's fixes live in, which needs nothing beyond Python.

Full install (client + server) — same command on Arch, Kali and Parrot

tools/install.sh detects your distro and installs whatever system packages it needs (GTK, PostgreSQL, etc.). Unchanged from upstream — see INSTALL.md for the distro-specific detail:

git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/king-phisher.git
cd king-phisher
sudo bash tools/install.sh

Just the dev/Python side (this fork's fixes, no GTK needed)

Only touches king_phisher.server and the shared code this fork fixed and tested — the GTK client itself still needs the full install above. Same command on Arch, Kali and Parrot once python3, pip and git are installed:

git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/king-phisher.git
cd king-phisher
tools/devshell.sh

That creates .venv/, installs requirements.txt into it, and drops you into a shell with it active.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Open a dev shell with the fork's dependencies installed

tools/devshell.sh

Run one command inside that environment without staying in it

tools/devshell.sh python3 -c "import king_phisher.server.database.models"

Start the server (full install only)

king-phisher-server -c server_config.yml

See upstream's wiki for configuring a campaign, the client, and template files — unchanged in this fork.

sections.label: Options
sections.html: tools/devshell.sh itself takes no flags: run it alone for an interactive shell, or tools/devshell.sh <command> to run one command inside the environment and return. Everything else — the server config file, the GTK client, campaign and template options — is upstream's, unchanged; see INSTALL.md and the wiki linked above.

sections.label: What's inside
sections.html:
PartWhat it isTouched by this fork
king_phisher/server/Server: SMTP sending, database, web server for landing pagesYes — the two fixes below
king_phisher/client/GTK campaign-editor and dashboard UINo
tools/install.shUpstream's full system installerNo
tools/devshell.shVenv lifecycle for the dev/Python sideAdded by this fork
requirements.txtDependency floors for the server/dev sideAdded by this fork

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream CrimsonForge-io/king-phisherThis fork
smtp_server.py on Python 3.12+Crashes on import (asyncore/smtpd removed by PEP 594)Rebuilt on asyncio via aiosmtpd, same public API
server.database.models importCrashes (sqlalchemy.Binary removed in SQLAlchemy 1.4+)Fixed: swapped for sqlalchemy.LargeBinary
Dependency versionsPipfile hard-pins ~40 packages to exact 2019 releases, no stated Python floorrequirements.txt with >= floors; verified installing and importing cleanly on Python 3.14
Dev environmentinstall.sh is a single sudo bash system installer, no venv storytools/devshell.sh: creates/updates a .venv, only ever active inside a subshell

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: smtp_server.py failed to import at all on Python 3.12+

It used the stdlib asyncore/smtpd modules, both removed by PEP 594 — upstream issue #522, where the maintainer confirmed the codebase is unmaintained and a from-scratch 2.0 is planned instead. Rebuilt on asyncio via aiosmtpd, keeping the same public API, and verified end-to-end against a real SMTP client on Python 3.14.

Fixed: sqlalchemy.Binary (removed in SQLAlchemy 1.4+)

Broke importing the whole king_phisher.server.database.models module and a historical Alembic migration. Swapped for sqlalchemy.LargeBinary — an identical column type, just renamed upstream — in both places.

Modernized: dependency floors

Added requirements.txt with the same roughly 40 packages upstream's Pipfile pins to exact 2019 releases, switched to >= floors so pip resolves current wheels. Verified on Python 3.14: every package installs cleanly and all 29 king_phisher.server submodules, plus the rest of the shared non-client code, import without error. One necessary cap: setuptools<81, because a transitive dependency (smoke-zephyr) still imports the now-optional pkg_resources API — documented inline in requirements.txt.

Added tools/devshell.sh: automated venv lifecycle

Upstream has no venv story (install.sh is a single sudo bash system installer). This script creates .venv/ on first run, installs or updates requirements.txt into it, and only ever activates the venv inside a subshell, so there's nothing to remember to deactivate — closing that shell, the command it ran, or the terminal all end it automatically.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html: This fork has no automated test suite of its own; the two fixes were verified directly: smtp_server.py against a real SMTP client end-to-end, and database.models by confirming all 29 server submodules import cleanly on Python 3.14 after the dependency changes.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• The GTK client needs system GObject-introspection libraries that are outside pip's scope and weren't available to verify in the environment this fork was built in; that part of INSTALL.md/tools/install.sh is unchanged from upstream and untested by this fork.
  • Campaign logic, templates, the web server for landing pages, and the rest of the server beyond the two fixes above are unchanged from upstream — including whatever else may not work on a Python this new, since upstream stopped testing against one.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: King Phisher sends real emails and serves real landing pages. Only run a campaign against an organisation that has authorized the test, with scope agreed in advance.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on king-phisher (formerly rsmusllp/king-phisher), by SecureState and its contributors. The server, client, campaign logic and templates are upstream's; the fixes above are this fork's.

sections.label: License
sections.html: BSD-3-Clause, the same as upstream. See LICENSE.

projects.name: ParamSpider
projects.tagline: Mines a domain's Wayback Machine history for every URL that ever carried a query parameter, so you have a fuzzing list without sending a single request to the live target.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: Before fuzzing or exploiting an endpoint, it helps to know which parameters it has ever accepted, without announcing yourself by probing it directly. ParamSpider pulls every archived URL for a domain from the Wayback Machine, strips out the noise (images, fonts, duplicate paths) and normalises every parameter value to a placeholder, leaving a clean, fuzzable URL list built entirely from passive data. This fork keeps that approach and fixes the parts that quietly lost data or killed a whole run over one bad domain.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Recon and enumeration: passive parameter discovery from archived data is a real step I use before active testing, not just a script I read.
  • Finding a logic bug that silently loses data, not just a crash: parse_qs() dropping every empty-value parameter doesn't error or print a warning, it just returns a shorter dict. Caught by comparing its output against the raw query string. See What changed.
  • Fixing a failure mode that only shows up at the scale the tool is meant for: one unresponsive domain in a 500-domain list used to take the other 499 down with it.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer (CI runs 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; also run by hand on 3.13 and 3.14)
  • requests, colorama (see requirements.txt)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
Arch Linux

sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/ParamSpider.git
cd ParamSpider
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/ParamSpider.git
cd ParamSpider
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .

Check it worked:

paramspider -h

The virtual environment only needs activating in the shell you use it from. Run deactivate, or open a new terminal, to leave it.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Mine one domain

paramspider -d example.com

Writes every parameterised URL found for the domain to results/example.com.txt.

Mine a list of domains

paramspider -l domains.txt

One domain per line. A domain the archive never answers is now skipped, not fatal to the rest of the list.

Watch the URLs as they're found

paramspider -d example.com -s

Route through a proxy

paramspider -d example.com --proxy '127.0.0.1:8080'

Use a reflection marker instead of FUZZ

paramspider -d example.com -p '"><h1>reflection</h1>'

Useful for a quick manual XSS sweep over the output file.

Give the archive more time to answer

paramspider -d example.com -T 60

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
FlagWhat it doesDefault
-d DOMAINDomain to minenone
-l FILEFile of domains, one per linenone
-sStream found URLs to the terminal as well as the fileoff
--proxy URLRoute requests through a proxynone
-p, --placeholder VALUEReplaces every parameter's value in the outputFUZZ
-T, --timeout SECONDSPer-request timeout30

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
Against a domain with three archived URLs (one an image, one with two empty-value parameters):

[INFO] Fetching URLs for example.com
[INFO] Found 3 URLs for example.com
[INFO] Cleaning URLs for example.com
[INFO] Found 2 URLs after cleaning
[INFO] Extracting URLs with parameters
https://example.com/profile?id=FUZZ&debug=FUZZ
https://example.com/search?q=FUZZ&token=FUZZ
[INFO] Saved cleaned URLs to results/example.com.txt

logo.png?v=2 was dropped as a static asset; debug and token, both archived with empty values, are kept.

sections.label: What it checks
sections.html:
ParamSpider doesn't check anything itself; it's a collector. What it does to each archived URL:

StepWhat happens
FetchEvery URL the Wayback Machine has ever archived for the domain, via the CDX API
Drop static assetsAny URL whose path ends in an image, font, stylesheet, script or document extension
NormaliseThe port stripped if it's the scheme's default, every parameter value replaced with the placeholder
DedupeIdentical normalised URLs collapsed to one, duplicate parameter names on one URL collapsed to one
Keep only parameterised URLsA URL with no ? is dropped from the output file

sections.label: How it works
sections.html: For a domain, it queries web.archive.org's CDX API for every URL ever captured under domain/*, which can be hundreds of thousands of entries for a large or old site. Each URL is parsed, static-asset extensions are filtered out, and every query parameter's value is replaced with the placeholder so that two archived requests to the same endpoint with different real values collapse into one fuzzable template.

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream devanshbatham/ParamSpiderThis fork
A parameter with no value (?token=&id=1)Silently dropped; only id survivesKept, same as every other parameter
Request timeoutNone; a slow or unresponsive archive.org request hangs forever-T/--timeout, default 30s
-l domains.txt when one domain's request fails after all retriessys.exit() kills the whole run, including every domain still queuedThat domain is skipped and logged; the rest of the list still runs
Output file orderArbitrary (set() iteration order); differs between identical runsSorted, same input always produces the same file
Automated testsNone9 tests, run in CI

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: empty-value parameters silently dropped

clean_urls() ran every URL's query string through urllib.parse.parse_qs(), which excludes any key whose value is empty by default. ?token=&id=1 became {'id': ['1']}, and token never appeared anywhere in the output — no error, no warning, just a parameter discovery tool that fails at discovering a parameter. Reproduced by feeding clean_urls() a URL with an empty-value parameter and checking it was missing from the result. Replaced parse_qs() with parse_qsl(..., keep_blank_values=True).

Fixed: no request timeout

client.fetch_url_content() called requests.get() with no timeout, so a request to archive.org's CDX endpoint that hung (which it does in practice; the endpoint is slow and sometimes unresponsive) blocked indefinitely with no way to recover. Reproduced against a local server that never responds: without a timeout the call hangs; with one it raises and the function retries instead of hanging forever. -T/--timeout (default 30s) is threaded through from the CLI.

Fixed: one failed domain killing the entire -l run

After exhausting its retries, fetch_url_content() called sys.exit(), which a caller has no way to catch or recover from: -l domains.txt with 500 domains where even one was unreachable killed the process and silently abandoned every domain still queued behind it. Reproduced with a mocked two-domain run where the first domain always fails: upstream never reaches the second domain. fetch_url_content() now returns None on exhausted retries, and fetch_and_clean_urls() logs and skips that domain instead of crashing.

Fixed: non-deterministic output order

clean_urls() built its result in a set() and returned list(cleaned_urls), whose iteration order is arbitrary and can differ between two runs over the exact same input, which makes the output hard to diff or deduplicate against a previous scan. It now returns sorted(cleaned_urls).

Housekeeping

The ASCII-art banner was a plain triple-quoted string containing \/, an invalid escape sequence that Python warns about on every run (SyntaxWarning: invalid escape sequence). Made it a raw string.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html:
pip install -r requirements.txt pytest
pytest -q

9 tests. A local HTTP server backs the timeout/retry tests (one endpoint that never responds, one that always 500s); the URL-cleaning tests run with no network access. GitHub Actions runs them on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• Entirely passive: a parameter that was never crawled by the Wayback Machine won't be found. Pair it with active tools (Arjun, in this list) for parameters the archive never saw.
  • Domain names from -l's file aren't validated or normalised beyond lower-casing and stripping a leading scheme; a line with a path or query string on it is passed to the CDX API as-is.
  • Retries use a fixed 5-second backoff with no rate-limit (429) awareness; a heavily rate-limited run just retries at the same pace.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: Only use discovered parameters against systems you own or have written permission to test. ParamSpider itself only talks to the Wayback Machine, never the target domain.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on devanshbatham/ParamSpider by Devansh Batham. Upstream's Wayback-mining approach and URL-cleaning logic are theirs. The fixes and tests above are in this fork.

sections.label: License
sections.html: MIT, the same as upstream. See LICENSE.

projects.name: Sherlock
projects.tagline: Finds a username across hundreds of sites, with a way to tell a confident hit from a false positive — upstream had no way to do that at all.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: A username-checker tool is only as useful as its false-positive rate. Sherlock's own detection can be fooled by a soft-404 page, a generic sign-in redirect, or a WAF challenge that still returns 200 — and it gave no way to tell a confident hit apart from one of those. This fork is built around fixing exactly that, plus the export bugs that lost data silently.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• OSINT: judging whether a tool's detection logic is actually trustworthy, not just whether it runs. --verify below is a method for catching a detector's own false positives, demonstrated against a real site.
  • Finding and fixing real data-loss bugs (the {?} wildcard and the --csv/--xlsx cases below), both reproduced before being fixed.
  • Contributing upstream: the export fixes are filed as sherlock-project/sherlock#3172, open at the time of writing.

sections.label: Requirements
sections.html:
• Python 3.10 or newer (upstream's CI covers 3.10 through 3.14)
  • Installed as an editable package via pyproject.toml (poetry-core build backend)
  • Tried on: Arch Linux, Kali Linux

sections.label: Install
sections.html:
This fork isn't on PyPI — that package name points to upstream — so install it from source.

Arch Linux

sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/sherlock.git
cd sherlock
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .

Kali Linux, Parrot OS

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git
git clone https://github.com/thecyberfarhan/sherlock.git
cd sherlock
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .

Check it worked:

sherlock --help

The virtual environment only needs activating in the shell you use it from. Run deactivate, or open a new terminal, to leave it.

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Check a username, with confidence flagged

sherlock --verify someusername

Re-checks every hit against a canary username; flags the ones that look like false positives.

Recover from a slow or rate-limited run

sherlock --retry 2 someusername

Re-checks only the sites that came back Unknown, up to 2 more times.

Export a structured report

sherlock --verify --export-json results.json someusername
sherlock --verify --markdown -o results.md someusername

Check one or two specific sites

sherlock --site GitHub --site Reddit --verify someusername

For the full site list and the rest of the base tool's flags, see upstream's own README (docs/pyproject/README.md) or the project site.

sections.label: Options
sections.html:
The fork-added flags (everything else is unchanged from upstream — run sherlock --help for the full list):

FlagWhat it doesDefault
--verifyRe-check every claimed hit against a canary username; mark low-confidence resultsoff
--retry NRe-check only Unknown sites, up to N more times0
--export-json FILENAMEWrite a structured JSON reportoff
--markdownWrite a .md table report, confidence flagged inlineoff

sections.label: Example output
sections.html:
Checking a real username against two sites, with --verify:

$ sherlock --site GitHub --site Reddit --verify torvalds

[+] GitHub: https://www.github.com/torvalds
[+] Reddit: https://www.reddit.com/user/torvalds
[*] Verifying 2 claimed result(s) against a canary username...
[!] Reddit: likely false positive (a random, unregistered username also came back "claimed" here)

[*] Search completed with 2 results

GitHub's detection held up. Reddit's didn't: a random, near-certainly-unregistered username also came back CLAIMED there, so the real result is flagged instead of presented as confident.

A --retry run recovering from a dead proxy:

$ sherlock --site GitHub --proxy http://dead-proxy:1 --retry 2 torvalds

[*] Checking username torvalds on:

[*] Retrying 1 site(s) that returned Unknown (attempt 1/2)...
[*] Checking username torvalds on:

[*] Retrying 1 site(s) that returned Unknown (attempt 2/2)...

A --markdown report, low confidence flagged inline:

| Site | Status | URL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | Claimed | [https://www.github.com/torvalds](https://www.github.com/torvalds) |
| Reddit | Claimed ⚠️ low confidence | [https://www.reddit.com/user/torvalds](https://www.reddit.com/user/torvalds) |

sections.label: How it works
sections.html: Sherlock requests a profile URL per site and decides "claimed" from the status code, a redirect target, or matching error text. --verify repeats that same check a second time against a randomly generated username that is near-certainly unregistered; if the site reports *that* username as claimed too, its detection can't actually distinguish a real account from a miss, so the original result is downgraded to low confidence instead of presented as a confirmed hit. This costs one extra request per site that claimed a hit, and none for sites that didn't, so the cost scales with how many hits came back.

sections.label: Comparison
sections.html:
Upstream sherlock-project/sherlockThis fork
Confidence on a hitNone — every claimed result is reported the same way, soft-404s included--verify flags low-confidence results
A transient error (timeout, rate limit)Reported Unknown and left there--retry N re-checks only the Unknown sites
A run where every request failsPrints "0 results", exit 0 — identical to a clean empty searchExplicit warning, exit 2
--output + a {?} wildcardSilently overwrites itself; only the last variant survivesRejected up front with a clear error*
--csv/--xlsx + --output/--folderoutputIgnored — always writes to the current directoryHonoured, same as every other export format*
Structured exportNone--export-json
Report format.txt, .csv, .xlsxAdds --markdown

\* Also submitted upstream as sherlock-project/sherlock#3172; if that's merged, those two rows stop being a difference.

sections.label: What changed
sections.html:
Fixed: --output silently lost results to a {?} wildcard

--output path is meant for a single username, but a {?} wildcard (name{?}) expands into several usernames before the write loop runs. Upstream checked the argument count *before* expansion, so name{?} looked like one username and was let through; each variant's result then overwrote the last one's output file. The check now runs against the expanded list and refuses up front with a clear error instead of silently losing data.

Fixed: --csv/--xlsx ignored --output and --folderoutput

Both writers always wrote to the current directory regardless of what was asked for; the Excel writer also ignored --folderoutput. Both now resolve through the same path logic as every other export format, so requesting several formats together doesn't make them overwrite each other.

Added: --verify, --retry, --export-json, --markdown

Described above. --verify runs once, after any retries, so a site that only succeeds on a retry still gets verified.

Changed: a total failure no longer looks like a clean empty search

If every request errors out (dead proxy, no network, aggressive rate limiting), Sherlock used to print "Search completed with 0 results" and exit 0 — identical to a genuine clean search. A run where every checked site comes back Unknown now prints an explicit warning and exits 2, so a script calling Sherlock can tell the two apart.

sections.label: Testing
sections.html: Upstream's own test suite (test_probes.py, test_manifest.py, test_unicode.py and the rest in tests/) runs unchanged; this fork doesn't touch detection logic, the site list, or proxy/Tor support, so it doesn't add to that suite. The flags above were verified by hand against real sites, shown in Example output.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• --verify roughly doubles the requests sent to sites that claimed a hit (none for sites that didn't), so a run with many hits takes longer.
  • Verification only catches a detector that can't distinguish a real account from a random one on the *same* site; it says nothing about sites not checked.
  • This fork doesn't touch detection logic, the site list, or proxy/Tor support — those are upstream's, unchanged.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: A username search is passive and touches only public profile URLs, but running it against someone without reason to is still a privacy intrusion. Use it for your own accounts, consented research, or an authorized engagement.

sections.label: Credits
sections.html: Built on sherlock-project/sherlock. The detection logic, site list, and base CLI are upstream's; the confidence check, retry logic, and export formats above are this fork's.

projects.name: Lab reports
projects.tagline: Pentest-style reports written against intentionally vulnerable training apps, in my own isolated lab.

sections.label: Why
sections.html: A finding is only half the job. The other half is writing it up the way a client actually reads it: what was tested, what was found, how bad it is, and how to fix it. These reports follow a real engagement's structure against apps built to be broken, so the structure can be shown without touching anyone else's system.

sections.label: What this shows
sections.html:
• Reporting: scope and rules of engagement, a summary a non-technical reader can act on, findings with evidence and risk ratings, and fixes in priority order — not just "I found a bug."
  • Using my own tools as part of a real engagement, not just running them standalone: the DVWA report's appendix is the actual reconkit and apicheck output from that test.
  • Confirming findings by hand, not trusting a scanner's output: the report says explicitly that the vulnerabilities were confirmed with minimal, safe proof-of-concept requests.

sections.label: What's inside
sections.html:
TargetAppStatus
DVWA (low security)Damn Vulnerable Web ApplicationDone
WebGoatOWASP WebGoatPlanned

Each report follows the same shape: scope and rules of engagement, a summary, findings with evidence and a risk rating, overall risk, and recommendations in priority order. The DVWA report additionally appendices the raw output of reconkit and apicheck run against the same target, as evidence of the recon phase that led to the findings.

sections.label: Method
sections.html: Black-box recon first (unauthenticated), then authenticated testing with the app's default low-privilege demo account. No automated exploitation tools were used against the live app beyond the two tools in this portfolio; every vulnerability below was confirmed by hand with minimal, safe proof-of-concept requests.

sections.label: Limitations
sections.html:
• Every target here is a training app built to be broken; findings and fixes reflect that, not a production system's full threat model.
  • Only one report (DVWA, low security setting) is complete; WebGoat is planned but not started.

sections.label: Responsible use
sections.html: All testing here is against instances run by me, on a network only I can reach. Nothing in this repo targets a system I don't own or don't have permission to test.
